questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: obtain the free-space wavelength of an EM wave from its frequency
questions.stem: A geostationary satellite downlinks data on a carrier of frequency 12.0 GHz. Using c = 3.0e8 m/s, what is the free-space wavelength of that carrier in metres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The relation c = f lambda inverts to lambda = c/f, so 3.0e8 m/s over 12.0e9 s-1 is 3.0e8/1.20e10 = 2.5e-2 m, which is 0.025 m. Rearranging the other way confirms it: c/lambda = 3.0e8/0.025 = 1.2e10 Hz = 12.0 GHz, the stated carrier. The tempting wrong answer multiplies instead of dividing, 3.0e8 x 12.0e9 = 3.6e18 m, which grows with frequency even though every real wavelength must shrink as the frequency rises.
questions.hint: Invert c = f lambda before substituting, since a bigger frequency means a smaller wavelength.

questions.learningObjective: identify which wave property is fixed by the source at a boundary
questions.stem: A monochromatic light wave of frequency 5.00e14 Hz travels in air and then enters a glass slab of refractive index 1.50. Which quantity is exactly unchanged by the crossing?

options.misconception: believes wavelength is conserved across a boundary

options.text: The frequency, which stays at 5.00e14 Hz

options.misconception: believes the vacuum speed survives inside matter

options.text: The wave number, which stays at 1.05e7 rad per m
options.misconception: confuses the wave number with the frequency

Picking wavelength, speed, or wave number fails because all three are set by the medium's response rather than by the source.

v = 1/sqrt(eps mu) = c/9.0 = 3.3e7 m/s, using the permittivity ratio directly
options.misconception: divides by the permittivity ratio and forgets the square root

options.text: v = eps mu c = 9.0 c = 2.7e9 m/s, so a high permittivity speeds light up
options.misconception: multiplies the speed by the material constants instead of inverting their root

options.text: v = c/1.0 = 3.0e8 m/s, since the permeability of 1.0 cancels any reduction
options.misconception: believes a nonmagnetic dielectric cannot slow a wave at all

Substituting eps = 9.0 eps0 and mu = 1.0 mu0 gives sqrt(eps mu) = 3.0 sqrt(eps0 mu0), and since c = 1/sqrt(eps0 mu0), the speed is c/3.0 = 3.0e8/3.0 = 1.0e8 m/s with a refractive index of 3.0. questions.topic: Field orientation in a plane wave
questions.learningObjective: apply the mutual perpendicularity of E, B, and propagation
questions.stem: A radar pulse travels along the positive x axis. At one instant the electric field of that pulse points along the positive y axis. In which direction does the magnetic field of the same wave point at that instant?

options.text: Along negative z, into the page in a right-handed view
options.misconception: takes the cross product in the left-handed order

options.text: Along positive z, out of the page in a right-handed view
Along positive x, the same way as the travelling pulse
options.misconception: confuses the wave with its own direction of travel

options.text: Along positive y, parallel to the electric field at that instant
options.misconception: assumes the two fields point in the same direction

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain why EM waves propagate in vacuum while mechanical waves do not
questions.stem: A water wave needs water to travel, yet a radio wave from a galaxy crosses 300 million kilometres of nearly empty space. Which statement best accounts for the difference?

options.text: A radio wave is a pattern of electric and magnetic fields, so it needs no particles to displace
A radio wave moves faster in vacuum because nothing there slows it down
options.misconception: treats the vacuum as merely a low-resistance medium for a mechanical disturbance

options.text: A radio wave carries its own particles, which is why it survives the emptiness
options.misconception: believes light travels as a stream of material particles through space

options.text: Water waves are slow only because water is heavier than empty space
options.misconception: blames the mass of the medium rather than the need for a medium

questions.explanation: A water wave is a displacement of matter, so remove the matter and the wave is gone. A radio wave is not matter in motion: it is a self-consistent oscillation of the electric and magnetic fields themselves, which Maxwell's equations permit in empty space, so the vacuum supports it perfectly well. The 300 million kilometres is 1.0 light-second at c = 3.0e8 m/s, which measures the travel time and proves nothing about a carrier medium. Option B is tempting because the speed really is 3.0e8 m/s in vacuum, but a mere absence of drag does not explain how a pattern travels at all.
questions.hint: Ask what is physically oscillating in each case, and whether it still exists in empty space.

questions.learningObjective: identify the circuit condition that radiates an EM wave
questions.stem: A physics class wants to detect the radio emission of a circuit with a small loop probe. Which arrangement will actually produce a measurable radiated wave?

options.text: A resistor carrying a steady current of 1.0 A for the whole hour
options.misconception: believes a large steady current is enough to radiate

options.text: A battery holding a constant 9.0 V across the resistor terminals
options.misconception: believes a stored voltage is enough on its own to radiate

options.text: A capacitor being charged and discharged at 1.0e9 times each second
A charged metal sphere sitting still on an insulating wooden stand
options.misconception: believes stored charge on an isolated body radiates

questions.explanation: Radiation comes from accelerating charge, so what matters is that the current changes, not that it flows. A capacitor cycled at 1.0e9 Hz accelerates its carriers back and forth 1.0e9 times each second, and that continual reversal is the radiation source, which is exactly how a radio transmitter works. A steady current, a constant battery voltage, and a stationary charged sphere all involve no acceleration of charge, so all three radiate nothing; the tempting belief is that large current, large voltage, or large stored charge is by itself sufficient.
questions.hint: Ask whether the charge carriers are speeding up, slowing down, or reversing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain what sustains an EM oscillation in charge-free space
questions.stem: Deep inside a beam of light in otherwise empty space there are no charges and no currents, yet the electric and magnetic fields keep oscillating. What sustains that oscillation?

options.text: Each changing field creates the other, so the pair regenerates itself indefinitely
The fields store energy from the source and simply release it without further input
options.misconception: treats stored field energy as self-sustaining without a conversion step

options.text: The vacuum itself acts as a medium with restoring forces on the field
options.misconception: invents a material vacuum medium that pushes the field back

options.text: The oscillating charges at the source pull on the fields across the whole distance
options.misconception: requires a continuing mechanical link back to the source

questions.explanation: Maxwell's two curl equations close on each other: a time-varying electric field acts as a source of magnetic field, and a time-varying magnetic field acts as a source of electric field. Option B is the appealing one and it fails on the conversion step: stored energy alone cannot manufacture a magnetic field out of a purely electric one, since the two must generate each other rather than merely run down.
questions.hint: Look for the pair of Maxwell laws that each names the other field as a source.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: compute the shortest wavelength an X-ray tube can emit from its voltage
questions.stem: An X-ray tube accelerates electrons through a potential difference of 40.0 kV. Taking h = 6.63e-34 J s, e = 1.60e-19 C, and c = 3.0e8 m/s, what is the shortest wavelength the tube can produce, in metres? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The largest photon energy available is the whole electron energy gain, eV = (1.60e-19 C)(4.00e4 V) = 6.40e-15 J, and the shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy, so lambda_min = hc/eV = (6.63e-34 J s)(3.0e8 m/s)/6.40e-15 J = 1.989e-25/6.40e-15 = 3.11e-11 m. Going the other way, f = E/h = 6.40e-15/6.63e-34 = 9.65e18 Hz and c/f = 3.0e8/9.65e18 = 3.11e-11 m, the same number. The tempting wrong answer reverses the dependence, pairing the maximum energy with the maximum wavelength, whereas E = hc/lambda means more energy always means less wavelength.
questions.hint: The largest photon energy the tube can make is eV, and lambda_min follows from E = hc/lambda.

questions.learningObjective: apply the 1/r^2 falloff of radiated intensity
questions.stem: A satellite downlink measures a signal intensity of 9.0e-14 W/m^2 at a range of 1.0e8 m. It then measures a target at 3.0e8 m along the same beam axis. What intensity does it measure in W/m^2? Assume free space with no losses and report the number only.
questions.explanation: Radiated power spreads over a sphere, so I = P/(4 pi r^2) falls as 1/r^2. Tripling the range from 1.0e8 m to 3.0e8 m therefore multiplies the intensity by 1/9, and 9.0e-14/9 = 1.0e-14 W/m^2. The full form agrees: P = (9.0e-14 W/m^2)(4 pi)(1.0e8 m)^2 = 1.13e4 W, and 1.13e4 W over 4 pi (3.0e8 m)^2 returns 1.0e-14 W/m^2. The tempting wrong answer 3.0e-14 W/m^2 divides by 3 instead of by 9, which is the 1/r rule a count rate follows, not 1/r^2.
questions.hint: Power spreads over a sphere, and a sphere's area grows as r squared.

options.text: I = eps0 c E0 squared over 2, and rms would divide that by 2 again

questions.explanation: The average intensity of a plane wave in vacuum is I = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2, and the 1/2 is the cycle average of sin^2, which is 1/2 over a full oscillation. Substituting rms amplitude, E_rms = E0/sqrt(2), into the equivalent form I = eps0 c E_rms^2 gives eps0 c (E0^2/2) = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2, the same number, so the peak form already carries the averaging and rms is not an extra factor of two. The claim that rms divides again is what the substitution just ruled out, and the linear form misses the squaring that turns amplitude into an energy rate.
questions.hint: The average of sin squared over a cycle is 0.5, which is where the factor of 2 goes.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: compute average intensity from a given electric field amplitude
questions.stem: A broadcast transmitter produces a plane wave in free space whose electric field amplitude is 1.0e2 V/m. Using eps0 = 8.85e-12 F/m, mu0 = 1.257e-6 H/m, and c = 3.0e8 m/s, what is the average intensity in W/m^2? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: I = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2 = 0.5 x (8.85e-12 F/m)(3.0e8 m/s)(1.0e2 V/m)^2 = 0.5 x 2.655e-3 x 1.0e4 = 13.3 W/m^2. The independent route through the magnetic field matches: B0 = E0/c = 1.0e2/3.0e8 = 3.33e-7 T, and I = c B0^2/(2 mu0) = 2.387e14 x 1.111e-13 = 26.5, halved to 13.3 W/m^2. The tempting wrong answer 26.6 W/m^2 omits the cycle-average factor of one half, and 0.133 W/m^2 is the error of treating intensity as linear in the amplitude rather than quadratic.
questions.hint: Use I = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2, or convert to B0 = E0/c and use I = c B0^2/(2 mu0).

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain why intensity depends on amplitude rather than frequency
questions.stem: A designer doubles the frequency of a broadcast transmitter from 50.0 MHz to 100 MHz and leaves the electric field amplitude at 1.0e2 V/m. What happens to the intensity in the far field?

options.text: It stays the same, because the relation to amplitude contains no frequency
options.misconception: does not recognise that intensity is frequency independent

options.text: It doubles, because a higher frequency carries more energy per wave
options.misconception: ties intensity to frequency at fixed amplitude

options.text: It stays the same, since 13.3 W/m^2 follows from the amplitude alone
It halves, because a higher frequency spreads the same power over a shorter wave
options.misconception: invents a 1/f law from the wavelength having halved

questions.explanation: I = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2 contains the amplitude and the vacuum constants, and c = 3.0e8 m/s for every frequency, so at fixed E0 the intensity does not depend on frequency: here 0.5 x 2.655e-3 x (1.0e2 V/m)^2 = 13.3 W/m^2 either way. The wavelength does halve, from 6.0 m to 3.0 m, but wavelength never appears in that expression. The belief that frequency must enter is a real confusion, since E = hf does raise the energy of each photon, but the number of photons arriving each second falls in step, leaving the energy flux unchanged.
questions.hint: Write I = (1/2) eps0 c E0^2 and check whether f appears anywhere in it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.topic: Detecting a law violation in data
questions.learningObjective: use an inverse-square law to find the inconsistent measurement
questions.stem: A ground station logs downlink intensity against range: 8.0e-14 W/m^2 at 1.0e8 m, 2.0e-14 W/m^2 at 2.0e8 m, 5.0e-15 W/m^2 at 4.0e8 m, and a second entry of 2.0e-14 W/m^2 also reported at 4.0e8 m. Which entry breaks the spreading law, and what should it read?

options.text: The duplicate 4.0e8 m entry, which should be 5.0e-15 W/m^2 from the inverse-square law
The 2.0e8 m entry, which should be 2.0e-14 W/m^2 from a linear falloff law
options.misconception: applies a 1/r law where 1/r^2 is required

options.text: The 1.0e8 m entry, which should be 2.0e-13 W/m^2 from the inverse-square law
options.misconception: treats the nearest range as the erroneous one

options.text: The 4.0e8 m entries, which should both be 1.0e-14 W/m^2 after halving
options.misconception: believes doubling the range only halves the intensity

questions.explanation: Free-space spreading gives I(r) = I(1.0e8 m) x (1.0e8 m/r)^2, so doubling the range divides the intensity by 4 and quadrupling it divides by 16. The 2.0e8 m reading checks out at 8.0e-14/4 = 2.0e-14 W/m^2 and the 4.0e8 m reading 5.0e-15 W/m^2 is 8.0e-14/16 as required, so the duplicate 2.0e-14 W/m^2 claim at 4.0e8 m is the outlier. It is a factor of 4 too high, which is exactly the error of dividing by 4 once instead of once per doubling of range.
questions.hint: Each doubling of range should divide the intensity by four, so check the sequence step by step.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: compute radiated intensity from power and range
questions.stem: A downlink antenna radiates 4.0e3 W uniformly in all directions. At a range of 1.0e8 m, what is the intensity in W/m^2? Use c = 3.0e8 m/s if needed and report the number only.
questions.explanation: An omnidirectional radiator spreads P = 4.0e3 W over a sphere of area 4 pi r^2 = 4 pi (1.0e8 m)^2 = 1.257e17 m^2, so I = P/(4 pi r^2) = 4.0e3/1.257e17 = 3.18e-14 W/m^2. Doubling the range to 2.0e8 m divides that by 4 to give 7.96e-15 W/m^2, which is the same answer reached from the ratio form I(r2) = I(r1)(r1/r2)^2 = 3.18e-14 x (1.0e8/2.0e8)^2. The tempting wrong answers 1.0e-13 W/m^2 drops the pi from 4 pi r^2, and 4.0e-21 W/m^2 is the error of using r cubed instead of r squared.
questions.hint: Intensity is the total power divided by the surface area of the sphere at that range.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: relate the resonant length of a rod antenna to the wavelength
questions.stem: A handheld radio works best at 150 MHz, where c = 3.0e8 m/s gives a 2.0 m wavelength. Its antenna is a single conducting rod, and the match is best when the rod length is what?

options.text: 2.0 m, one full wavelength of the 2.0 m wave, for maximum efficiency
options.misconception: equates a full wavelength with the resonant rod length

options.text: 1.0 m, one half of the 2.0 m wavelength, the usual quarter-wave scale
options.misconception: pairs a half wavelength with a quarter-wave label

options.text: 0.10 m, one twentieth of the wavelength, keeping the rod compact
options.misconception: believes a short stub still resonates at the carrier

options.text: 0.50 m, one quarter of the 2.0 m wavelength, a resonant monopole length

questions.explanation: A thin rod couples power most strongly at lengths that are a resonant fraction of the wavelength: a full-wave dipole is lambda = 2.0 m, and the quarter-wave monopole that works against a ground plane is lambda/4 = 0.50 m, the classic handheld length. Off resonance the rod's inductance and end capacitance no longer cancel its reactance, so the transmitter cannot push power into it at 150 MHz. Choosing lambda/2 confuses the monopole scale with the dipole scale, and 1/20 of a wavelength is far too short to resonate.
questions.hint: A handheld rod antenna works against the ground plane it sits on, which sets the fraction of a wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: state what it means for a wave to be linearly polarized
questions.stem: A polarizer transmits only the component of a wave's electric field that lies along its transmission axis. What does it mean to say that a wave is linearly polarized?

options.text: Its electric field oscillates in every transverse direction at once, equally
options.misconception: describes an unpolarized beam as though it were polarized

options.text: Its electric field oscillates along one fixed direction as the wave advances
Its electric and magnetic fields oscillate along the same fixed direction
options.misconception: believes the two fields are parallel to each other

options.text: Its electric field oscillates at a constant rate that never changes direction
options.misconception: confuses a constant frequency with a polarization

questions.explanation: Polarization names the fixed direction, lying in the plane transverse to propagation, along which the electric field of that wave oscillates, and rotating a polarizer about the beam axis brightens the transmitted wave up to a maximum exactly when its axis matches that direction. Oscillating equally in every transverse direction describes an unpolarized beam, which is why the first polarizer always passes half of it. Fields oscillating in the same direction would break the perpendicularity between E and B, and a constant rate with no direction is simply a frequency, not a polarization.
questions.hint: Turn the polarizer about the beam axis and watch what the transmitted brightness does.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: chain two polarizers using the halving rule and Malus's law
questions.stem: Unpolarized light of intensity I0 strikes a first polarizer, then a second polarizer whose axis is turned 30 degrees from the first. In terms of I0, what intensity leaves the second polarizer?

options.text: I = 0.5 I0 cos squared 30 = 0.375 I0, halving then applying Malus
I = I0 cos squared 30 = 0.75 I0, applying Malus with no halving
options.misconception: skips the halving done by the first polarizer

options.text: I = 0.5 I0 cos 30 = 0.433 I0, halving then taking the cosine
options.misconception: omits the square that Malus's law requires

options.text: I = 0.5 I0 sin squared 30 = 0.125 I0, halving then using sine
options.misconception: swaps the roles of crossed and aligned axes

questions.explanation: The first polarizer has no axis to respect in unpolarized light, so it passes exactly half, I1 = 0.5 I0. The second then follows Malus's law with the 30 degree angle between the two axes: I = 0.5 I0 cos^2(30 degrees) = 0.5 I0 x 0.75 = 0.375 I0. Omitting the halving gives 0.75 I0, which is the value you would read if the light entering the first polarizer were already polarized, and using the sine instead swaps a crossed pair for an aligned one and returns 0.125 I0.
questions.hint: Deal with the first polarizer by the halving rule, then use Malus's law for the angle.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain the rotation-independence of a single ideal polarizer
questions.stem: A beam of unpolarized light of intensity 6.0 W/m^2 is sent through a single ideal polarizer that the operator then turns slowly through a full turn. What does the meter behind it read?

options.text: A steady 6.0 W/m^2, because one polarizer cannot remove any light
options.misconception: believes an ideal polarizer is lossless

options.text: A steady 1.5 W/m^2, because a quarter of the light is lost at each edge
options.misconception: invents a fixed quarter loss at every polarizer surface

options.text: A steady 3.0 W/m^2, because an unpolarized beam has no preferred axis
A reading swinging between 0.0 W/m^2 and 6.0 W/m^2 as it turns
options.misconception: applies Malus's law to light that is not polarized

questions.explanation: Unpolarized light is an equal mixture of every polarization direction, so whatever orientation the polarizer holds, the transmitted fraction is the same: I0/2 = 3.0 W/m^2. There is no preferred axis in the incoming beam for the rotation to exploit, which is exactly why Malus's law needs a stated angle between two axes and cannot be used here. The swinging reading is what a second polarizer placed after the first would show, and losing a quarter of the light is not a physical step in an ideal polarizer.
questions.hint: Ask whether the incoming beam has a polarization axis for the rotation to line up with.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain how a receiving wire responds to field orientation
questions.stem: A vertically polarized broadcast is received by a straight wire antenna held vertical, and the wire is then rotated to horizontal. What changes at the receiver?

options.text: The coupling falls toward zero, because the wire responds to the field along its length
The coupling is unchanged, because the field strength is the same in both positions
options.misconception: assumes antenna orientation cannot matter at all

options.text: The coupling doubles, because a perpendicular wire collects more of the wave
options.misconception: believes a crossed wire receives the maximum signal

options.text: The coupling falls to zero, because a horizontal wire sits outside the wave
options.misconception: claims the horizontal wire is outside the wave entirely

questions.explanation: A straight conductor responds to the electric field component along its own length, because only that component drives charge back and forth in the wire. With the broadcast's electric field vertical, a vertical wire is aligned and couples strongly, while a horizontal wire is perpendicular to that field and induces almost no voltage, so the received signal collapses even though the wave's energy still passes by. Option D overstates the result: the horizontal wire is not outside the wave, it is simply blind to that field direction and still re-radiates what it picks up.
questions.hint: Ask which component of the electric field can push charge along the length of the wire.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_EM
questions.learningObjective: explain why reflected glare can be reduced by a polarizer
questions.stem: Sunlight reflecting off a wet road at a shallow angle looks harsh, and polarized sunglasses cut the glare noticeably. Which fact about that reflection makes the polarizer worth using?

options.text: The reflected light has a much shorter wavelength, so the filter blocks that band
options.misconception: believes reflection shortens the wavelength of the light

options.text: Reflection at a shallow angle partially polarizes the light, favouring one axis
The reflected light carries a different frequency, so the filter rejects that one
options.misconception: believes reflection shifts the frequency of the light

options.text: The reflected light is simply more intense, so the filter cuts the extra power
options.misconception: treats a polarizer as a device for cutting excess power

questions.explanation: At a grazing angle the reflected beam is partly linearly polarized in the plane of incidence, so a polarizer set to pass that direction still transmits much of the sky's unpolarized light while rejecting a large share of the road's polarized glare. Reflection at a fixed-angle mirror leaves the wavelength and frequency untouched, so the two spectral explanations describe effects reflection does not have, which is why a band-pass idea never helped glare. The last option inverts the argument: a polarizer removes a preferred direction, it does not remove power, and the sky light passes it unharmed.
questions.hint: Think about what grazing-angle reflection does to the polarization of the beam it sends back.
